results.result: The stomach continuously produces a slow electrical rhythm at 0.05 Hz (one cycle every 20 s) that is intrinsically generated by interstitial cells of Cajal in the stomach wall, which form synapse-like connections with both gastric smooth muscle and afferent sensory neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C6 are all supported by appropriate citations to established literature (Koch and Stern 2004; Bozler 1945; Suzuki et al. 1986; Sanders et al. 2014; Powley and Phillips 2011). These claims establish the physiological basis for the gastric rhythm that is central to the study and are well-documented in prior work.

results.result: Visceral inputs can reach cortical targets, gastric frequency (~0.05 Hz) falls within the range of BOLD fluctuations used to define resting-state networks and is free from known cardiac and respiratory artifacts, and the amplitude of alpha rhythm depends on the phase of gastric rhythm.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C10 are supported by appropriate citations (Critchley and Harrison 2013; Park and Tallon-Baudry 2014; Glerean et al. 2012; Richter et al. 2017). These claims provide the rationale for why gastric-brain coupling is a plausible phenomenon to investigate and are based on established prior work.

results.result: The mean EGG peak frequency across 30 participants was 0.047 Hz (±SD 0.003, range 0.041–0.053), and EGG peak frequency measured inside and outside the scanner did not differ.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C12 are directly supported by the study data with appropriate statistical testing (t(28)=0.35, p=0.725, Bayes Factor <0.001). The control measurement outside the scanner validates that the MRI environment does not distort the gastric frequency measurement, which is an important methodological control.

results.result: Significant phase coupling between the EGG and resting-state BOLD time series occurred in twelve nodes comprising the right primary somatosensory cortex, bilateral secondary somatosensory cortices, medial wall motor regions, extrastriate body area, posterior cingulate sulcus, dorsal precuneus, ventral and dorsal occipital cortex, retrosplenial cortex, and superior parieto-occipital sulcus, with shared variance between EGG and BOLD signals ranging from 12% to 16.9%.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C23 are supported by appropriate statistical analysis (voxel threshold p<0.01, cluster threshold corrected for multiple comparisons, Monte-Carlo p<0.05) and are presented with detailed anatomical localization in Table 1 and Figure 2a. The use of cluster-based permutation testing with multiple comparison correction is appropriate. The shared variance estimates (12-16.9%) are reasonable for this type of analysis.

results.result: Gastric-BOLD coupling strength was not significantly related to gender, body mass index (BMI), or trait anxiety scores.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C26 are supported by appropriate statistical testing (ANCOVA with F-statistics and p-values reported). However, the manuscript notes that BMI variation in the sample was limited (all participants had BMI < 25), which limits the generalizability of this finding. The Bayes factors support the null hypothesis, strengthening the conclusion.

results.result: Summary statistics decreased when shifting the filter below or above the gastric peak frequency, indicating that the gastric network corresponds to BOLD fluctuations specifically occurring at gastric frequency.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C28 are supported by the frequency specificity analysis shown in Figure 2b. This control analysis demonstrates that the observed coupling is specific to the individual gastric frequency rather than being a general low-frequency phenomenon, which strengthens the interpretation that the coupling is genuinely related to gastric rhythm.

results.result: The probability of the gastric network results being a false positive is less than 0.001.
results.evaluation: Claim C29 is supported by the surrogate data analysis in which 1000 random time shifts were applied to the EGG signal and none produced summary statistics as large as the original data. This is a rigorous control for false positives, though the exact probability estimate depends on the assumption that the surrogate procedure adequately captures the null distribution.

results.result: The gastric network is specific to individual gastric peak frequency, is highly unlikely to be a chance finding, is not dependent on BOLD power, and is not linked to spurious effects of head movement on the BOLD signal.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C37 are supported by multiple control analyses with appropriate statistical testing and Bayes factors indicating decisive evidence for the null hypotheses where appropriate. The controls for BOLD power (t(29)=1.19, p=0.24), head movement (t(29)=-0.34, p=0.73), EGG power (F(1,28)=0.9, p=0.51), and EGG peak frequency (F(1,28)=1.6, p=0.17) are comprehensive and strengthen confidence in the main findings.

results.result: The gastric network includes the right primary somatosensory cortex in the hand and mouth region (mostly overlapping with area 1, 60.2% of the SIr node) and bilateral secondary somatosensory cortices (right SII mostly overlapping with area OP1, 35.2%; left SII overlapping with both OP1, 21.7% and OP4, 14.9%), overlapping with body maps classically associated with touch.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C42 are supported by anatomical overlap analysis with cytoarchitectonic subdivisions. The quantitative overlap percentages are reported and the interpretation that the gastric network overlaps with somatotopic body maps is reasonable. However, the functional significance of this overlap is interpretive rather than directly demonstrated.

results.result: Gastric-BOLD coupling was found in the posterior bank of the parieto-occipital sulcus (dOcc and vOcc) and retrosplenial cortex, regions where a previous MEG study showed that the amplitude of the alpha rhythm was modulated by gastric phase.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C44 are supported by the current study data (C43) and citation to prior work (Richter et al. 2017, C44). The convergence between the current fMRI findings and prior MEG findings strengthens the interpretation that gastric-BOLD coupling has a neural origin, though this remains an inference rather than direct demonstration.

results.result: Only the right posterior insula showed evidence for gastric-BOLD coupling across participants in a region-of-interest analysis (t(29)=2.78, p=0.043, Bonferroni corrected), with an effect size (Cohen's d = 0.84) within the lower range of the gastric network (mean Cohen's d = 1.19 ± 0.21 STD, ranging from 0.80 to 1.62).
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C47 are supported by appropriate statistical testing with Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons across 6 insular subdivisions. The effect size analysis provides useful context for interpreting the relative strength of coupling in the insula compared to other nodes. The finding that the insula shows weaker coupling than most other nodes is noteworthy given its known role in visceroception.

results.result: 30% of the gastric network was related to heart rate variability, with very limited overlap (4.7%) with known sympathetic areas, and 17% of the gastric network overlapped with regions correlating with pupil diameter, though coupling strength did not correlate with shared pupil-EGG variance (r = 0.05, p=0.82, BF = 0.17).
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C52 are supported by appropriate overlap analyses and statistical testing. The partial overlap with autonomic regulation areas (heart rate variability, pupil diameter) is quantified, and the lack of correlation between coupling strength and pupil-EGG variance (C52) suggests that the gastric network is not simply reflecting general autonomic arousal. However, the pupil analysis was conducted on only 20 participants due to data loss.

results.result: Temporal delays of ~3.3 s occurred between the earliest nodes (somatosensory cortices) and latest nodes (dorsal precuneus and EBA) of the gastric network, with the right posterior insula showing delays in the range of the earliest nodes, and different nodes were coupled to the gastric rhythm with significantly different phase delays (F(11, 29)=5.22, p<10⁻⁶), indicating a precise temporal sequence of activations within each gastric cycle.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C56 are supported by phase-delay analysis with appropriate statistical testing (Watson-Williams test for circular data). The finding of systematic temporal delays across nodes is a key novel aspect of this study. However, the interpretation of these delays as reflecting a 'precise temporal sequence of activations' (C56) is somewhat inferential, as the delays could also reflect differences in hemodynamic response timing or other factors.

results.result: Delayed functional connectivity between gastric nodes (mean 40.8% ± SD 8%) was systematically larger than instantaneous functional connectivity (mean 30.2% ± SD 11%, paired t-test, t(29)=9.02, p<10⁻¹⁰), indicating that in contrast to classical RSNs, the gastric network is characterized by between-node delayed connectivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C58 are supported by appropriate statistical testing comparing delayed and instantaneous functional connectivity. The finding that delayed FC is systematically larger than instantaneous FC is a key distinguishing feature of the gastric network compared to classical RSNs. The statistical evidence is strong (p<10⁻¹⁰), and the interpretation is reasonable.

results.result: Episodes of elevated gastric-BOLD synchronization corresponded to episodes of increased BOLD amplitude, with time-varying PLV and BOLD time series significantly correlated in all gastric nodes (Bonferroni corrected p<0.006, mean r = 0.18 ± 0.02), and the correlation between time-varying PLVs for all possible node pairs was significantly positive at the group level (t(29)=9.22, p<10⁻¹⁰, mean r = 0.129 ± 0.075), indicating that slow temporal fluctuations in gastric-BOLD coupling are associated with changes in BOLD amplitude and occur simultaneously in all nodes.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C62 are supported by time-varying PLV analysis with appropriate statistical testing. The finding that fluctuations in coupling strength are associated with BOLD amplitude changes and occur simultaneously across nodes provides insight into the temporal dynamics of the gastric network. However, the correlations are modest (mean r = 0.18 for C60, mean r = 0.129 for C61), suggesting that other factors also contribute to these fluctuations.

results.result: Canonical RSNs based on instantaneous connectivity represent only one of the possible partitions of the brain into coherent networks based on temporal dynamics.
results.evaluation: Claim C63 is a broad interpretive conclusion that is reasonably supported by the overall findings of the study, particularly the demonstration of a network characterized by delayed rather than instantaneous connectivity. However, this is a single example, and the generalizability of this conclusion to other potential delayed-connectivity networks remains to be demonstrated.

results.result: The stimulation of the splanchnic nerve that innervates the stomach evokes responses in contralateral SI and bilateral SII in several mammals, the spinothalamic tract targets MWM in monkeys, vagal stimulation can evoke responses in somato-motor cortices, and single neurons with convergent visceral and hand inputs have been observed in SI.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C67 are supported by appropriate citations to prior work (Amassian 1951; Dum et al. 2009; Ito et al. 2003; Brüggemann et al. 1997). These claims establish the anatomical basis for direct gastric inputs to the early nodes of the gastric network and are well-documented in the literature.

results.result: SIr, SII and MWM could be the entry point of gastric afferences.
results.evaluation: Claim C68 is a speculative inference based on the phase advance of these regions and known anatomy (C64-C67). While the inference is reasonable, it is not directly demonstrated by the current data. Alternative explanations (e.g., differences in hemodynamic response timing) are not fully ruled out. The claim is appropriately presented as speculative ('could be').

results.result: The right posterior insula, which receives direct cardiac inputs in monkeys and is considered a visceral cortex, was found to be coupled with the stomach, though the modest involvement might be due to the absence of an interoceptive task, as BOLD signal in the insula increases when participants explicitly monitor a visceral variable.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C72 are supported by appropriate citations (Zhang et al. 1998; Critchley et al. 2004) and the study data (C45-C47). The interpretation that the modest insula involvement might be due to the absence of an interoceptive task (C71) is speculative but reasonable. However, this remains an untested hypothesis.

results.result: Regions receiving direct visceral inputs are also early nodes of the gastric network, suggesting that the BOLD fluctuations locked to the gastric rhythm have a neural origin, with additional support from the finding that neural activity in the alpha range is modulated by gastric phase in parieto-occipital regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C75 are supported by the phase-delay analysis (C53-C56) and citation to prior work (Richter et al. 2017). The convergence of evidence from phase delays, known anatomy, and prior MEG findings supports the interpretation of a neural origin. However, this remains an inference, and alternative explanations (e.g., vascular mechanisms) are not completely ruled out, though they are addressed in C76-C82.

results.result: Artefactual BOLD fluctuations caused by head movements driven by stomach contractions seem unlikely, as gastric-BOLD coupling was neither related to head movement nor to EGG power; during digestion, gastric blood flow varies but cerebral blood flow is unaltered; artificial distension of the stomach can cause increases in peripheral blood pressure, but this is mostly due to catheter insertion rather than inflation; spontaneous blood pressure fluctuations occur at ~0.1 Hz (Mayer waves), which is much faster than gastric rhythm; thus, a vascular effect seems unlikely, and the hypothesis that activity in the gastric network is driven by neural activity in areas directly receiving ascending inputs appears more plausible.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C83 are supported by the control analyses (C30-C33) and appropriate citations (Matheson et al. 2000; Gallavan et al. 1980; Min et al. 2011; Cantù et al. 2008). The argument against vascular artifacts is reasonably comprehensive, though not definitive. The conclusion that neural mechanisms are more plausible (C83) is a reasonable inference but not a direct demonstration.

results.result: The functional role of the coupling between stomach and body maps might be related to homeostatic regulations, and more specifically, the gastric network might be involved in the regulation of digestion, which is accompanied by changes in cardiac output and heart rate.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C86 are speculative interpretations of the functional role of the gastric network. While the partial overlap with heart rate variability regions (C48) provides some support, these claims are not directly tested in the current study. The speculation is reasonable but remains hypothetical. Claim C86 is supported by citation (Kelbaek et al. 1989).

results.result: The EBA is not purely visual but is also activated during movement, imagination, and haptic recognition of body parts; primary somatosensory cortex combines internal and external bodily information by receiving both tactile and visceral afferents; medial wall motor regions receive visceral inputs in addition to containing motor maps; thus, activity in 5 out of 12 nodes of the gastric network could be explained by a representation of the stomach in brain body maps.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C91 are supported by appropriate citations (Astafiev et al. 2004; Kitada et al. 2009; Costantini et al. 2011; Brüggemann et al. 1997; Follett and Dirks 1994; Levinthal and Strick 2012). The interpretation that activity in 5 nodes could be explained by stomach representation in body maps (C91) is a reasonable inference based on the established multisensory nature of these regions.

results.result: The gastric network comprises regions that play a role in mapping external space in bodily coordinates (right superior parieto-occipital sulcus, dorsal precuneus, RSC), with the superior parieto-occipital sulcus encoding visual stimuli in bodily coordinates during action, and the dorsal precuneus and RSC implementing integration of information into an egocentric reference frame; all 12 nodes but three (posterior cingulate sulcus, ventral and dorsal occipital clusters) either contain body maps or map external information in bodily coordinates.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C95 are supported by appropriate citations (Bernier and Grafton 2010; Burgess et al. 2001; Vann et al. 2009) and established functional knowledge of these regions. The characterization of the functional properties of the gastric network nodes is reasonable, though the functional significance of their involvement in the gastric network remains interpretive.

results.result: The gastric network might coordinate different body-centered maps, with the function of gastric-BOLD coupling in nine areas being to co-register body-centered maps of the body and external space; foraging and feeding behaviors are likely candidates for tasks in which the gastric network would play a role; in SI and EBA, gastric-BOLD coupling is maximal in the hand and mouth region, suggesting a potential link with feeding behavior.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C99 are speculative interpretations of the functional role of the gastric network. While the anatomical and functional characterization of the nodes (C92-C95) provides some support, these functional hypotheses are not directly tested. Claim C99 is supported by the anatomical overlap analysis (C38-C42), but the link to feeding behavior remains speculative. These are reasonable hypotheses for future testing.

results.result: Delays in resting-state functional connectivity have been highlighted only recently but have long been documented in stimulus-induced BOLD responses; within functionally coherent systems, delays of 2 s are common; long delays are unlikely to directly reflect synaptic delays of fast sequential neural transmission (10-15 ms per stage), though longer delays might occur if local recurrent processing is involved; delays might reflect regional differences in vascular response timing, slow changes in neural activity (accumulation processes), or neuromodulatory influences, which might affect cerebrovascular reactivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C108 are supported by appropriate citations (Yellin et al. 2015; Mitra and Raichle 2016; Saad et al. 2001; Kruggel et al. 1999; Thorpe et al. 1996; Krimer et al. 1998). The discussion of potential mechanisms underlying the observed delays is appropriately cautious and acknowledges multiple possibilities. However, the current study does not distinguish between these mechanisms.

results.result: If the gastric network plays a role in homeostasis, interactions are likely to be bidirectional; medial wall motor regions both receive inputs from the spino-thalamic tract and generate sympathetic outputs; the gastric-locked modulation of the alpha rhythm in ventral and dorsal occipital clusters was previously shown to be mostly due to ascending influences from the stomach to the brain.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C111 are supported by established anatomical knowledge (C110) and citation to prior work (Richter et al. 2017, C111). Claim C109 is a reasonable inference about bidirectional interactions in homeostasis, though the current study does not directly test directionality. The PLV measure used is not a directed measure, as the authors acknowledge.

results.result: RSNs have been defined as segregated systems that show synchronous fluctuations during rest; the gastric network, albeit distinct from classical RSNs, falls under this definition and can be considered a novel RSN that could not be previously observed due to methodological reasons.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C114 are supported by citation to the definition of RSNs (Fox and Raichle 2007, C112) and the overall findings of the study. The conclusion that the gastric network is a novel RSN (C114) is reasonable, though the claim that it 'could not be previously observed due to methodological reasons' is somewhat overstated—it could also be that previous studies did not look for delayed connectivity networks.

results.result: Delays are an intrinsic characteristic of brain dynamics unfolding in anatomically connected networks and are pervasive even at the timescale of BOLD signal fluctuations.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C116 are supported by appropriate citations (Deco et al. 2011; Mitra et al. 2015). These claims provide context for the finding of delayed connectivity in the gastric network and are well-established in the literature.

results.result: Thirty-four right-handed participants took part in the study, with four excluded (two due to excessive head movement and corrupted EGG data, two due to unclear EGG spectral peaks), resulting in 30 participants (mean age 24.2 ± 3.31, 15 females, mean BMI 21.48 ± 1.91) who fasted for at least 90 min before recordings and underwent a 900 s resting-state scan with eyes open fixating on a bull's eye.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C121 are directly reported from the methods section. The sample size (n=30) is reasonable for this type of study, though the authors note it was powered to detect medium effect sizes. The exclusion criteria are appropriate and clearly stated. The fasting period (90 min) is relatively short, which may have influenced the results.

results.result: The gastric network is a novel, delayed-connectivity resting-state network in humans that cuts across classical resting-state networks with partial overlap with autonomic regulation areas, is composed of regions involved in mapping bodily space through touch, action or vision and mapping external space in bodily coordinates, and is characterized by a precise temporal sequence of activations within a gastric cycle, beginning with somato-motor cortices and ending with the extrastriate body area and dorsal precuneus.
results.evaluation: Claims C122-C125 represent the main conclusions of the manuscript and are supported by the comprehensive set of analyses presented (C13-C23, C38-C42, C48-C52, C53-C56, C57-C58, C92-C95). The characterization of the gastric network as a novel RSN with delayed connectivity is well-supported, though some aspects of the functional interpretation remain speculative.

results.result: With long time scales, RSNs closely match the anatomical backbone of the brain; with short time scales (~10-100 s), spontaneous brain activity is characterized by the emergence and dissolution of network patterns with rich temporal trajectories; temporal trajectories indicate the existence of delays between regions, whereas standard methods (seed-based correlation and independent component analysis) make the implicit assumption that RSNs are characterized by instantaneous or zero delay connectivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C126-C130 are supported by appropriate citations (van den Heuvel et al. 2009; Honey et al. 2009; Shen et al. 2015; Ponce-Alvarez et al. 2015; Shine et al. 2016; Mitra et al. 2015) and established knowledge of standard methods (C130). These claims provide important context for the novelty of the current study's approach to identifying RSNs based on delayed connectivity.
